passage: For much of the twentieth century, forest agencies in several countries treated fire as an enemy to be defeated wherever it appeared. The logic seemed unanswerable: fire destroys timber, threatens homes and kills animals, so every fire extinguished was a loss averted. Agencies measured their performance by how quickly they put fires out and how few hectares burned, and by those measures many of them succeeded remarkably well. Lookout towers, firebreaks and crews ready to move at short notice made it possible to reach most fires while they were still small.

The success contained its own reversal. In many dry forests, frequent fires of low intensity had once cleared the undergrowth, fallen branches and young trees that gather on the forest floor, while leaving the older, thick-barked trees largely unharmed. When such fires were suppressed year after year, that material was left to build up. The forest grew denser, and the fuel that would once have burned off in small, manageable fires accumulated until, in a hot, dry season, a fire that could not be stopped found enough of it to climb into the crowns of the trees. Such fires kill the very trees that the earlier, smaller ones had spared. By preventing many small fires, suppression had, in effect, been saving up for a few enormous ones.

The lesson is sometimes drawn too broadly. Not every ecosystem evolved with frequent fire; in some wet forests and many shrublands fire was historically rare, and a recent increase in burning there is a threat rather than a return to normal. Nor does the history of suppression explain every catastrophic fire, since drought, heat and the spread of housing into wooded land matter as well. The argument is not that fire is good, but that whether a given fire is harmful depends on the ecosystem in which it burns and on that ecosystem's history.

Recognising this has not made the remedy easy. Deliberately setting fires under controlled conditions, or allowing some natural fires to burn, can reduce accumulated fuel, but it carries risks that suppression appeared not to. Politically, a season without burning looks like competence. Smoke drifts over towns, and a planned burn that escapes is blamed on the people who lit it, while a wildfire that grows from decades of accumulated fuel is blamed on nature. A manager therefore faces an asymmetry. The harm of acting is visible and attributable; the harm of not acting is deferred and diffuse, and the easiest course is to keep doing what made the problem worse.

options.A: the planting of fast-growing, thin-barked trees in place of the older species of dry forests.
options.B: the build-up of undergrowth and fallen branches in dry forests after decades of fire suppression.
options.C: the spread of houses and settlements into land that is covered by woods and forest.
options.D: long spells of drought and heat in the seasons when the most destructive fires break out.

passage: Elections are so closely identified with democracy that it can seem perverse to ask whether they are democratic at all. Yet consider what an election rewards. To win, a candidate must stand out from the crowd: be better known, better funded, better connected or simply more persuasive on a platform than the people whose votes are sought. An election is, in this sense, a procedure for picking a distinguished few, and the chambers it fills tend to resemble the electorate less closely than a random sample of that electorate would. Many ancient Greek writers saw the point clearly; for them, filling offices by lot was the characteristically democratic method, and election was a device that favoured the prominent.

The modern case for selection by lot builds on that old intuition. A body drawn at random from the adult population brings into the room the people who are usually spoken about rather than heard: the shift worker, the pensioner, the young parent who would never run for anything. Its members owe nothing to donors or to party managers, since nobody campaigned to put them there. Above all, they are free to change their minds. An elected representative who revises a position after hearing the evidence risks being called a turncoat; a citizen chosen by lot has no platform to betray, and so can treat a question as something to be worked out rather than a position to be defended.

Critics usually reply that ordinary citizens lack the competence to legislate. This objection is weaker than it sounds. Few elected legislators are experts in more than a sliver of what they vote on; they rely on staff, committees and witnesses, and there is no reason a randomly chosen body could not do the same. A more serious difficulty concerns accountability. An elected member who disappoints can be removed at the next election, and the prospect of removal disciplines conduct in between. A member chosen by lot answers to no one, and the very independence that shields such a member from donors also shields him or her from voters. Those who propose replacing elected chambers with lotteries have not, to my mind, answered this objection.

The sensible conclusion is not that lot should displace election but that it can do something election does badly. On some questions elected politicians have every incentive to avoid committing themselves, because any clear answer will cost them votes. A panel chosen at random, given time, evidence and a duty to hear opposing witnesses, can show what ordinary people conclude once they have actually thought the matter through, and its recommendations can then be put to the legislature or to the voters for decision. The lottery's virtue is that it reveals considered public judgement; its limit is that no one has authorised the people it selects to rule.

options.A: Legislators who disappoint their voters are often re-elected anyway, because voters remain loyal to the party under whose name they stand.
options.B: Elected legislators who depend heavily on staff and committees are often captured by those advisers, and end up voting as the advisers recommend.
options.C: Panels chosen by lot, unlike legislators, prove unable to judge which of their expert witnesses are reliable, and tend to adopt the view of whoever spoke last.
options.D: Most elected legislators possess specialist knowledge of at least one policy area, usually drawn from the occupation they followed before entering politics.

passage: Marketers like to say that the strongest brands have communities rather than customers. They point to the owners of a particular make of motorcycle who ride together on weekends and have its emblem tattooed on their arms, to the users of a computer maker's products who queue overnight for a new model and argue online with the users of its rivals, and to the enthusiasts who restore and exhibit a discontinued car long after its manufacturer has stopped caring about it. Some commentators go further and call such groups tribes, or even congregations, complete with rituals, myths and heretics, as though buying a product were the first step in a conversion.

The comparison is not empty. Members of these groups share a body of lore, the founding story, the legendary models, the right and wrong ways to use the product, and newcomers learn it much as initiates learn a tradition. They define themselves partly against outsiders, often the owners of a rival brand, and they police their own boundaries, distinguishing the real enthusiast from the person who has merely bought the thing. Most strikingly, they develop a sense of ownership over the brand that is not legal but moral. When a company alters a celebrated design or moves production to another country, its most loyal customers frequently respond not as disappointed consumers but as betrayed members, as though something that belonged to them had been taken without their consent.

Yet the tribal analogy conceals as much as it reveals. Membership of a tribe is not usually something one buys, and leaving it is not usually as easy as buying something else. A brand community, by contrast, is entered through a purchase and can be abandoned at the price of another. More important, the symbols around which it gathers are the legal property of a firm whose interests are not the members' interests. The firm can redesign the emblem, discontinue the product or sell the brand to a competitor, and the members, however devoted, have no formal say in any of it. A tribe whose totem could be sold at auction would be a strange tribe indeed.

It is tempting to resolve the tension by declaring one side the truth: either the community is an illusion manufactured by advertising, or the commercial setting is incidental and the solidarity is all that matters. Neither will do. The solidarity is real; people form friendships, give one another practical help and find meaning in these groups, and much of this happens without the company's involvement or even against its wishes. But the solidarity is organised around something its members do not control, and that fact shapes it. The anger that follows an unpopular redesign is the anger of people discovering, often for the first time, the limits of an ownership they had felt but never possessed.

A brand community, then, is best understood neither as a tribe that happens to shop nor as a market that happens to feel warm, but as a peculiar hybrid: a genuine collective built on borrowed ground. Firms that grasp this tend to treat their communities with caution, consulting them, deferring to them on matters of heritage and sometimes ceding them real influence over decisions. Firms that do not, and that treat the community merely as a marketing asset to be managed, are apt to learn how quickly devotion can turn into grievance, and how little the language of community protects a firm once its members conclude that they have been treated as an audience rather than as partners.

options.A: As disappointed consumers who decide to transfer their loyalty to the brand of a rival firm.
options.B: As members who feel that something of theirs has been taken from them without their agreement.
options.C: As enthusiasts who quietly accept the change because the product remains largely the same.
options.D: As owners who take legal action to stop the company from altering the products they bought.

options.C: Members of a computer brand's online forums spend considerably more each year on the brand's products than its other customers do, and buy new models sooner.

passage: Every alliance contains a quiet bargain between two fears. A state that joins an alliance worries, on the one hand, that its partner will fail it when it is attacked: this is the fear of abandonment. It worries, on the other, that its partner will drag it into a war it has no wish to fight, over interests that are not its own: this is the fear of entrapment. The two fears pull in opposite directions, and much of what passes for the routine management of alliances, the ministerial visits, the joint statements, the careful wording of guarantees, is an effort to keep them in tolerable balance.

The difficulty is that almost anything done to ease one fear aggravates the other. A state that tightens its commitment, by stationing troops on its partner's soil or promising automatic assistance, reassures the partner that it will not be abandoned. But the same assurance may embolden the partner to take risks it would otherwise avoid, confident that its ally will be obliged to follow. Loosening the commitment has the opposite effect: it restrains the partner, but it also invites the partner to doubt the alliance and perhaps to look for other friends, or to arm in ways that alarm its neighbours. There is no setting of the dial at which both fears disappear, and governments that search for one tend to lurch between them, reassuring an anxious ally one year and reining in an emboldened one the next.

For this reason, the ambiguity of many alliance commitments, often criticised as a failure of nerve, is better seen as a deliberate instrument. A guarantee that is firm enough to deter an adversary but vague about the circumstances in which it will be honoured leaves the protecting power room to judge whether its partner has provoked the crisis. The partner, uncertain whether reckless conduct will be supported, has reason to be careful; the adversary, uncertain whether aggression will be resisted, has reason to be careful too. Consider a hypothetical great power that promises to defend an island partner but declines to say whether the promise covers a dispute the partner itself might start. The silence is not an oversight. It is the policy.

The balance between the two fears is rarely the same for both members. A small state facing a powerful neighbour usually fears abandonment far more than entrapment, since it has few other places to turn, while its larger protector, with interests elsewhere and wars it would prefer not to fight, tends to fear entrapment more. Much of the friction within alliances that look harmonious from outside comes from this asymmetry: the junior partner asks for firmer pledges, the senior partner resists giving them, and each suspects the other of bad faith when each is in fact responding sensibly to its own position.

Ambiguity is not free, however. Its value depends on each party reading the uncertainty in the way the protecting power intends, and there is no guarantee that they will. An adversary may conclude that a vague commitment is a hollow one and test it, discovering too late that it was real. A partner may conclude that it will be supported whatever it does, because it cannot imagine its patron allowing it to fall. Deliberate vagueness thus trades the visible risks of a firm commitment for the hidden risk of miscalculation, which is the more dangerous for being invisible until a crisis reveals it. The strategy rewards a protecting power that understands both its partner and its adversary well, and punishes one that merely hopes it does.

options.A: A shopkeeper who offers a generous guarantee on every item she stocks sells more goods but must then pay to repair the ones that break.
options.B: An employer who keeps the terms of a bonus vague so that staff keep working hard without counting on any fixed reward.
options.C: A parent's promise to pay all of a grown child's debts reassures but invites borrowing; withholding it curbs borrowing but leaves the child feeling deserted.
options.D: A teacher who sets a very difficult examination finds that the strongest students in the class rise to it while the weakest ones simply give up.

passage: When two researchers, one celebrated and one unknown, publish a discovery together, the discovery is very likely to be remembered as the celebrated researcher's. The same pattern appears when two people arrive at a result independently: the one who is already eminent tends to receive the larger share of the attention, the citations and the invitations that follow. Sociologists of science named this the Matthew effect, after the verse in the Gospel of Matthew about those who have being given more, and it is usually discussed as a problem of fairness. The unknown co-author did much of the work, and someone else collected the credit.

That description is correct within its limits, but it understates what is at stake, and it also misses why the effect is so persistent. Scientists face a literature far larger than anyone could read in a lifetime. A familiar name on a paper is a cheap signal that the paper is probably worth the reader's time, and in a world of scarce attention, readers who rely on such signals are not being foolish. To some degree, then, the effect is the by-product of a reasonable strategy for coping with abundance. Condemning it as mere snobbery does not explain why careful and fair-minded people take part in it every day.

The trouble begins when attention is converted into resources. A researcher whose papers are widely read finds it easier to win grants, which pay for students and equipment, which produce more papers, which are read more widely still. Advantage compounds. After a few rounds, the difference between two careers may bear little relation to any difference in the quality of their first ideas, and the field as a whole has placed a heavy bet on one line of work for reasons that are partly accidental. Ideas that happened to originate with the less visible researcher may wait years for a hearing, or never receive one, not because they were tested and found wanting but because nobody with the means to test them was looking in their direction.

Seen in this light, the effect is less an injustice done to individuals than a distortion in how a field allocates its bets, and the remedy is not to forbid readers from noticing names, which would be both futile and costly. It is to loosen the link between attention and money: to judge some grant proposals without knowing who wrote them, to set aside funds for researchers early in their careers, and to treat a famous name as a reason to read a paper rather than as a reason to believe it.

options.A: rejecting it entirely, on the ground that credit in science is in fact distributed according to merit.
options.B: endorsing it fully, since the author regards the effect chiefly as an injustice done to unknown researchers.
options.C: accepting it as accurate as far as it goes, while holding that it misses the more serious harm.
options.D: treating it with open contempt as a complaint voiced only by those who have themselves been denied credit.

passage: Spoken irony rarely needs announcing. A slight drag on a word, a flattened pitch, a pause before the punchline: listeners pick up such cues without noticing that they have done so, and the speaker relies on them without noticing either. Writing, however expressive in other respects, strips most of them away. For centuries this mattered less than it might have, because the written forms people used for personal exchange, letters above all, were slow, composed and long enough to establish their own tone over several paragraphs. A letter writer who wished to be ironic had room to prepare the reader for it.

The short typed message removes that room while keeping the pace of speech. Exchanges happen in seconds, between people who often know each other well enough to joke, in fragments too brief to carry their own context. The result is a familiar variety of communicative accident. A remark meant as affectionate teasing arrives as a rebuke; a dry agreement reads as sincere enthusiasm, or the reverse. The writer, who heard the intended tone in his own head as he typed, is often the last to see that it was not on the screen.

Writers have not, however, accepted this deprivation quietly. Over the past few decades they have built, without any committee to guide them, a supplementary system of signals: the small faces and symbols that can be appended to a sentence, the strategic use of capitals and repeated letters, even the presence or absence of a full stop, which among some groups of writers has come to make a short reply sound curt. It is common to lament these devices as a decline in the standards of written language. That complaint misses what they are for. They are not a lazy substitute for vocabulary but a written prosody, an attempt to restore precisely the cues that typing removed.

Yet the new system has a weakness that spoken prosody largely lacks. The meaning of a rising tone is shared across most speakers of a language; the meaning of a particular symbol or a missing full stop is settled within smaller circles and changes quickly. A face that one group uses to soften a criticism may strike another as mocking, and a message read across a gap of age or community can misfire precisely because the writer took care to mark its tone. The invention of written prosody, in other words, has not abolished misreading so much as relocated it, from the gap between voice and text to the gap between the conventions of different readers.

options.A: critical, because the view mistakes devices for restoring tone for mere carelessness.
options.B: approving, because the author regards the signals as too local and unstable to count as a proper part of written language.
options.C: neutral, because the author reports the view without indicating any judgement about it.
options.D: sympathetic, because the author agrees that the signals are less precise than a well-chosen word.

passage: It is often said that overconfidence is the most pervasive of the biases, the one from which many of the others draw their strength. The claim is repeated so often that it is easy to miss how much it conceals. 'Overconfidence' names at least three different things, and they do not always travel together. Treating them as one has made the phenomenon seem both more universal and more mysterious than it is.

The first is overestimation: believing that one has performed, or will perform, better than one actually does. The second is overplacement: believing that one is better than other people. The third, which receives less public attention, is overprecision: excessive certainty that one's beliefs are accurate, shown when people asked for a range they are ninety per cent sure contains some true value give ranges that contain it far less often than that. These sound like variations on a single vanity, but they come apart in revealing ways. On tasks that are easy, people tend to underestimate how well they have done, even as they place themselves above others; on tasks that are very hard, the pattern reverses, and many people will rate themselves below average at, say, juggling or composing verse while still overestimating their own scores.

What explains such reversals is less a desire to think well of oneself than the way information is distributed. People usually know more about their own performance than about other people's, so their judgements of others are pulled toward a vague middle. When a task is hard, they sense that they did poorly, if not quite how poorly, but assume that others did less badly; when it is easy, the opposite. A good deal of what looks like ego, in other words, is a predictable consequence of reasoning from imperfect information about the people with whom one is being compared.

Overprecision is different. It shows no comparable tendency to reverse, appearing on easy and hard questions, among novices and among specialists, and it is the form that does most harm in planning, where projects are budgeted against ranges too narrow to include what actually happens. It is also the form that most resists exhortation: telling forecasters to be humble rarely widens their intervals much. More promising are procedures that change the question, such as asking people to assign probabilities to several ranges in turn, so that the possibility of an outcome far from their best guess must be considered explicitly rather than waved away. The lesson is not that confidence is good or bad but that a single word has been doing the work of three, and that each of the three needs its own diagnosis.

options.A: judge both their own scores and their standing relative to others accurately, because poor results are obvious.
options.B: give much wider ranges for their estimates than they do on easy tasks, so that their overprecision disappears.
options.C: rate themselves below average compared with others while still overestimating their own scores.
options.D: rate themselves above average compared with others while underestimating how well they have actually done.

passage: A persistent habit of literary talk treats the short story as a smaller novel: the same materials of character, setting and incident, simply supplied in lesser quantities. On this view the story is where writers practise before attempting the larger form, and a collection of stories is a kind of portfolio of novels not yet written. The habit is reinforced by publishers, who have long regarded collections as harder to sell, and by critics who praise a story for being 'as rich as a novel', as though richness of that kind were the measure of success. Prizes and anthologies have sometimes followed suit, treating a writer's stories as preparation and the first novel as the real debut.

The comparison misunderstands where a short story does its work. A novel accumulates; it earns its effects through duration, letting the reader live alongside its people for enough days that change in them can be felt as change. A story has no such time to spend. What it has instead is selection, and selection pressed hard enough becomes a kind of meaning in itself. When a story shows a woman packing a suitcase, pausing over a single photograph and putting it back in the drawer, the eleven years of marriage that the story never describes are present precisely because they are withheld. The reader does not receive them; she supplies them, and the supplying is the experience.

This is why expanding a fine story so rarely improves it. Give the woman a history, a sister to confide in, a chapter on the courtship, and the photograph becomes one detail among many rather than the point on which everything turns. The gaps that had been doing the work are filled with information, and information, however well written, is less charged than implication. The reader who had been supplying the marriage is now simply told about it, and being told is a lesser kind of participation. The story's brevity was not a limitation it laboured under but the condition of its force.

None of this means that stories and novels never meet. Some writers have plainly used stories as sketches, and more than one long novel began as a few pages its author could not leave alone. Nor is brevity a virtue in itself; a weak story can hide behind its shortness, gesturing at depths it has not earned. The claim is narrower: that when a story succeeds on its own terms, it succeeds by a method the novel mostly cannot use, and that judging it by the novel's standards will reliably mistake its strengths for omissions.

options.A: Writers who began with short stories and later turned to novels often say that the shorter form taught them economy.
options.B: Publishers continue to report that collections of short stories sell fewer copies than novels by the same writers.
options.C: Several admired novels are known to have grown out of rough, unfinished short pieces that their authors went on revising, sometimes for many years, before finally publishing them.
options.D: Readers comparing admired stories with later full-length versions by the same writers mostly found the longer versions stronger, because of the added history.

passage: The maxim that there is no disputing about taste is usually offered as a courtesy. When two people disagree about a film or a piece of music, one of them, sensing that the conversation is about to turn sour, observes that it is all a matter of taste, and the other, relieved, agrees. The maxim seems to express a modern and admirable humility, for who is anyone to tell another person what to enjoy? But the courtesy rests on a confusion, and the confusion has consequences for the way we talk about art and, in the end, for the way we treat one another.

The confusion is between preference and judgement. If you dislike the taste of coriander and I like it, there is nothing for us to argue about. Neither of us thinks the other has missed something; we simply report different reactions, and the reports do not compete, any more than your being cold and my being warm in the same room amounts to a disagreement about the room. Disagreements about novels or buildings are rarely like this. When I say that a novel is sentimental and you say that it is moving, each of us means to be saying something about the book, and each of us expects the other to be able, at least in principle, to recognise it. We point to passages, compare the novel with others, and draw attention to what the other may have overlooked. These are the moves of people who believe there is something to be right about, even if neither of them can prove it.

The relativist replies that this behaviour, however common, rests on an illusion. There is no fact about the book's sentimentality independent of readers' reactions, the argument runs, and so our disputes, unlike disputes about the boiling point of water, can never be settled; at most one party tires and gives up. This reply assumes that a dispute is worth having only if it can end in proof. Aesthetic argument, however, does not aim at proof. It aims at a change in perception, and its success is the moment when you look again at the passage I have pointed to and hear the false note I heard, or when I, rereading it at your insistence, find that what I took for manipulation is in fact restraint. Such moments are not rare. Most people can remember a friend, a teacher or a critic who showed them something they had not been able to see, and they do not remember the experience as having been talked into a preference; they remember it as having learned something.

It must be granted that some disagreements reach a floor. Two careful readers may agree about every feature of a poem, its rhythm, its imagery, its debts and its departures, and still differ about whether it is good, because one prizes austerity and the other abundance. At this point argument may genuinely run out, and it is sensible to say so. But the floor lies far lower than the maxim implies. Most disputes about taste break off long before they reach it, not because the parties have exhausted their reasons, but because one of them has invoked the maxim in order to end the conversation.

There is, finally, something less humble in the maxim than it appears. To tell someone that their view of a novel is merely a matter of taste is to decline to treat it as a view at all, that is, as a claim that might be true and from which one might learn. The maxim protects both parties from the risk of being wrong, but it does so at the price of the possibility of being changed. Real respect for another person's judgement would consist in disputing it.

options.A: some disputes persist even when both parties agree about every feature of a work, because they value different qualities.
options.B: most disputes about taste end only after the parties have exhausted every reason they have.
options.C: some disputes about a work become so heated that the parties refuse to continue them, though both still have reasons to give.
options.D: aesthetic argument can in the end yield proof of the kind that the relativist demands of it.

passage: It is easy to write the history of urban smell as a simple story of progress. Pre-modern cities stank of sewage, tanneries, slaughterhouses and unwashed bodies; reformers built drains and water supplies; the stench retreated. Every part of this is true, and anyone inclined to romanticise the crowded streets of earlier centuries should be reminded of it. But the story assumes that the nose is a constant instrument, registering the same smells with the same disgust in every age, and that assumption does not survive a reading of the sources.

Residents of older towns certainly complained about smells, but their complaints were selective. Odours that later generations would find unbearable, such as the smell of a dung heap beside a house, were often accepted as part of ordinary life, while others, associated with particular trades or with neighbours who were disliked, drew sustained protest. What made a smell intolerable depended less on its strength than on what it was thought to mean. And from the late eighteenth century onwards, in much of Europe, smells came to carry a very specific meaning with new urgency. Under the old theory that disease spread through foul air, now taken up by physicians and reformers, a bad smell was not merely unpleasant; it was a warning, perhaps even the danger itself.

The theory was wrong, but it was productive. Because it identified smell with sickness, it gave reformers a reason, and a sense of urgency, to remove the sources of smell, and many of the measures they took, from covered sewers to the regular removal of refuse, did reduce disease, though for reasons they did not understand. A mistaken idea about how illness spread thus helped to justify works whose real benefit lay elsewhere. When the germ theory displaced it, smell lost its medical authority; it did not lose its power.

Freed from medicine, the vocabulary of smell attached itself more firmly to persons. Middle-class households that had learned to fear foul air now learned to fear the odour of the poor, the newcomer and the manual worker, and the judgement passed easily from bodies to character. The cleaner cities became, the more a lingering smell could serve as a mark of social distance. This is why a history of smell cannot be only a history of drains; it must also be a history of who was allowed to call whom offensive, and of how a sense that seems the most immediate of all has always been schooled.

options.A: was stronger than the ordinary smells of household refuse and animal dung that residents lived beside.
options.B: came from the drains and sewers that reformers had recently built to carry waste away from the streets.
options.C: was linked in residents' minds with a particular trade or with neighbours they disliked.
options.D: was believed by physicians to carry disease, since every bad smell was then treated as a medical danger.

passage: When readers began, in large numbers, to write and circulate their own stories about the characters of popular novels and television series, the reaction from some authors was indignation. The characters were theirs, they said; to send them on adventures their creators had never imagined, to pair them with new lovers or to bring the dead back to life was a kind of trespass. Defenders of the practice replied with equal heat that a story, once released into the world, belongs to those who love it, and that the fans who keep a fictional world alive with their own inventions have a better claim to it than the person who merely began it. Both sides, I think, have misdescribed what is at stake.

Consider first how unusual the authors' position is, historically speaking. For most of the history of storytelling, retelling was the ordinary way in which stories lived. The same heroes passed from one teller to another, gaining episodes, companions and endings along the way; a poet who took up an old legend was expected to change it, and was admired for the changes. The idea that a fictional person belongs to a single creator, and that others may not set that person in new situations, took shape alongside printing, markets for books and laws that made authorship a form of property. It is not a natural fact about stories, though it now feels like one. Fan writers, from this angle, are less the vandals of a settled order than the late heirs of a much older one.

Yet the fans' champions claim too much when they turn this history into a counter-theory of ownership. To say that a story belongs to those who love it is still to speak of belonging, merely moving the title deeds from one party to another. What the older practice suggests is rather that stories are not the sort of thing that is owned in the first place, though particular tellings are. An author can reasonably object to having her text copied and sold under someone else's name, or to having her own work altered and passed off as hers. It is much harder to see what she loses when a reader imagines her characters on another afternoon, so long as no one mistakes that afternoon for one she wrote. The distinction between a text and a world is precisely the one that both sides have blurred.

There is an irony here that deserves notice. Fan communities, which began by contesting an author's exclusive authority, have often developed authorities of their own. Long debates arise over what counts as 'canon', over which inventions are faithful and which are betrayals, and newcomers who ignore the accumulated rules can be treated with a severity that few authors would dare to show their readers. In such moments the community reproduces, on a smaller scale, the very proprietary attitude it set out to resist, as though the impulse to fix a story and guard its boundaries were not peculiar to authors but a temptation that comes with loving any story at all.

None of this settles every case, and there are surely retellings that wound in ways the distinction does not capture, as when a living author's characters are put to uses she finds degrading. But it does suggest a more useful question than the one with which the quarrel began, which asked whose story it is. The better question is what each kind of claim protects: the integrity of a particular telling, which deserves defence, or the boundaries of an imagined world, which, on the evidence of the long history of storytelling, have never been defensible for long.

options.A: A poet retells an ancient legend that she too once retold, adding new episodes and a different ending.
options.B: A reader writes and circulates a story in which two of her minor characters fall in love on holiday.
options.C: A fan community holds long debates over which events in her series ought to count as canon.
options.D: A reader alters several chapters of the author's novel and circulates them, under the author's name, as the original text.

passage: Anthropologists have long described rites of passage as moving in three phases. The person undergoing the rite is first separated from an existing status, then passes through a transitional period in which he or she belongs to neither the old condition nor the new, and is finally incorporated into the community in a new role: adult, married, initiated, ordained. Of these phases the middle one, often called liminal, from the Latin word for a threshold, has attracted by far the most attention, and for good reason. It is there that most of the strange features of such rites are concentrated: seclusion in the forest or a special hut, the shaving of heads, the wearing of identical plain garments, the suspension of names, the imposition of hardship and silence.

A simple reading treats these features as a waiting room, a pause while the real change, the conferral of new status, is prepared offstage. This misses their function. Stripping novices of names, clothing and possessions removes the markers by which they were previously ranked, so that for a time sons of important families and sons of poor ones are indistinguishable. Shared hardship then does two things at once. It makes the novices receptive to instruction, since people deprived of their usual footing listen differently, and it binds them to one another in a way that often outlasts the ritual, creating cohorts whose loyalty cuts across lineage and wealth.

In recent decades, however, the idea has travelled far from its origins, and something has been lost on the way. The liminal phase is now often celebrated as a zone of freedom, creativity and play, and the word is applied to almost any in-between experience: the years after school, a period of unemployment, a long journey abroad. This enthusiasm overlooks how tightly the traditional threshold was managed. Elders set its length, prescribed what novices could eat and say, and decided when it was over. Its ambiguity was real, but it was ambiguity held inside a firm frame, and its whole point was the return.

That frame is what most modern transitions lack. A young person who drifts between education and employment may experience the disorientation of the threshold without its discipline, its companions or, above all, its exit. There is no moment at which the community declares the passage complete and receives the person in a new capacity. None of this implies that the old rites should be revived, since their authority rested on forms of social life that no longer exist. But the comparison suggests that what made liminality productive was not the openness that its modern admirers praise. It was the certainty that the openness would end.

options.A: Elders in some traditional societies extended the seclusion of novices who had broken the rules of the rite.
options.B: Young people passing through open-ended, unmarked transitions are found to form lasting ties and take on new roles just as well as novices in bounded rites do.
options.C: Many young people who drift between education and employment say that they feel disoriented, lack companions and cannot tell when, if ever, their transition will be over.
options.D: In some societies the period of seclusion during initiation lasted several years rather than a few weeks.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's conclusion about what made liminality productive?

passage: Public debate about bureaucracy tends to oscillate between two complaints. One is that officials are rigid, applying rules mechanically to people whose circumstances the rules never anticipated. The other is that officials are arbitrary, treating similar applicants differently according to mood, prejudice or the length of the queue. The usual remedy for the second complaint is more rules: tighter eligibility criteria, standard forms, checklists that leave nothing to judgement. Each new scandal of favouritism produces another layer of instructions, and the layers accumulate. The remedy is seldom questioned, because it seems obvious that a rule applied uniformly is fairer than a person deciding as he pleases.

What this remedy overlooks is that the officials who deal directly with the public, the benefits clerk, the housing inspector, the teacher deciding which pupil needs extra help, cannot stop exercising judgement however detailed their instructions become. A rule says that an applicant must provide proof of address; it does not say how hard the clerk should look for an acceptable document when the applicant has been living with relatives. Moreover, such officials almost always have more cases than time. They must decide whose file to open first, whose story to probe and whose to accept, and these decisions shape outcomes as surely as any formal ruling. When rules are tightened, judgement does not disappear. It retreats into these less visible choices, where it is harder to observe and correct.

This is not to romanticise frontline discretion. The same latitude that allows a sympathetic clerk to find a way through for a desperate family allows an unsympathetic one to find reasons for delay, and there is ample reason to think that such latitude is not exercised evenly across applicants of different backgrounds. The case for discretion is not that officials can be trusted. It is that the choice is not between discretion and its absence, but between discretion that is acknowledged and discretion that is driven underground. Discretion of the first kind can be examined and improved; discretion of the second kind can only be suspected.

Seen this way, the task of administrative reform changes. Instead of writing rules ever more finely in the hope of closing every gap, an agency might record the informal decisions its staff actually make, review samples of cases to see how similar applicants fare, and give officials explicit guidance on the purposes their judgement should serve. None of these steps would remove judgement from the counter; they would make it something an agency can see, discuss and, where necessary, correct. Such measures concede what the rule-writer prefers to deny: that every system of rules ends, at its edges, in someone deciding.

options.A: After an agency introduces a fixed scoring sheet, supervisors begin publishing how often each caseworker's applicants are approved and refused.
options.B: After an agency introduces a fixed scoring sheet, its caseworkers come to differ chiefly in how quickly they schedule interviews for the different applicants they serve.
options.C: After an agency introduces a fixed scoring sheet, its caseworkers openly refuse to use it and carry on assessing applicants exactly as they did before.
options.D: After an agency introduces a fixed scoring sheet, fewer applicants are approved, because the new sheet is stricter than the assessments it replaced.

passage: Suppose the history of life could be rewound to some early point and allowed to run again. Would anything like the present living world appear a second time? One school answers no. Evolution, on this view, is a chain of contingencies, each step dependent on the particular steps before it and on unrepeatable accidents of climate, geology and mutation. Alter any early link, and the chain would run off in another direction entirely; the existence of vertebrates, of flowering plants or of our own species would be no more to be expected than a particular sequence of cards in a shuffled deck. On this view the tree of life is a record of accidents, intelligible after the fact but not predictable before it, and any search for a direction in it reads our own presence back into a history that never had us in mind. The rival school points to the remarkable frequency with which evolution arrives at the same solution independently. Camera-like eyes have arisen separately in vertebrates and in octopuses; streamlined bodies have evolved in fish, in extinct marine reptiles and in dolphins; flight has been achieved by insects, pterosaurs, birds and bats. If the same designs keep recurring, the argument runs, the outcome of a second run would be broadly familiar.

Each school has a strong case, and each tends to treat the other's evidence as anecdote. Convergence enthusiasts can list hundreds of cases, but the list is assembled after the fact from the solutions that did recur, and it says nothing about the far larger number of forms that appeared once and never again. Contingency enthusiasts can point to those unrepeated forms, but they often treat the mere fact that a lineage had a particular history as proof that its outcome depended on that history, which does not follow: a ball may take a unique path down a hillside and still come to rest in the only hollow at the bottom.

Much of the disagreement, I want to suggest, dissolves once we notice that the two schools are describing life at different levels of detail. At the level of broad functional solutions, a second run would very probably produce organisms that see, swim, fly and filter food, because the physical problems of moving through water or air, or of forming an image from light, admit only a few good solutions. At the level of particular lineages, the replay would almost certainly differ: there is no reason to expect that the flying creatures would be birds, or that the swimmers would have backbones. Convergence is a claim about the space of workable designs; contingency is a claim about which occupants of that space history happens to supply. The two are compatible, and both are probably true.

This reconciliation has a cost, and it is worth stating plainly. If the question that matters is whether a replay would produce something like us, a self-aware animal that makes tools and uses language, then neither school's best evidence is decisive. Intelligence of our kind has arisen, so far as we know, only once, and a single case cannot reveal whether it was a likely destination or a fluke. The recurrence of eyes and wings tells us that some problems have few solutions; it does not tell us that every capacity we value is among those solutions. On the questions that most excite the public, the honest answer is that the evidence does not yet discriminate between the two views.

options.A: the history of a lineage is of no use in understanding what that lineage became.
options.B: an end point reached by a route no one could repeat may still have been very likely to be reached.
options.C: contingency enthusiasts are wrong to claim that many forms appeared only once.
options.D: the outcomes of evolution are fixed in advance by the physical shape of the environment.

options.A: partisan, favouring the convergence school and treating the contingency school's case as anecdote.
options.B: even-handed, crediting each with a real insight while faulting how it treats evidence.
options.C: dismissive, regarding the entire debate between them as confused and not worth pursuing.
options.D: deferential, accepting the claims of each school and declining to judge between them.

options.C: irrelevant to any question about what a replay of evolution would be likely to produce.

passage: Among the stories collected in the Zhuangzi, one of the best known concerns an enormous tree. A master carpenter passes it without a second glance, and when his apprentice asks why so magnificent a specimen has been ignored, he explains that its wood is good for nothing: boats made from it would sink, coffins would rot and tools would split. That night the tree appears to the carpenter in a dream and rebukes him, pointing out that trees bearing fruit are stripped and broken and never live out their natural years; its own uselessness, it explains, is precisely the reason it has lived so long and grown so large.

The usual moral drawn from the story is a prudent one: in a dangerous world, conspicuous talent invites exploitation, and the wise keep their heads down. That reading has support in the text, which elsewhere praises figures who survive by escaping notice. But it makes the story smaller than it is. The carpenter's mistake is not merely that he underrates the tree; it is that he assumes the only question worth asking about a tree is what it is good for to a carpenter. The tree's reply amounts to the observation that usefulness is always usefulness to someone, for some purpose, and that a thing seen only through that lens is not really seen at all.

This point has lost none of its edge. We are surrounded by institutions that measure things by their contribution to some further end, and we have grown skilled at the carpenter's glance. A subject of study is asked to justify itself by the jobs it leads to, a stretch of land by the revenue it can produce, an hour of a person's time by what it yields. Each of these questions is reasonable on its own, and institutions that never asked them would be failing in their responsibilities. What the story warns against is letting one of them become the only question, so that whatever cannot answer it, a friendship, a landscape, an afternoon of unhurried conversation, is passed by as if it were not there.

It would be a mistake, though, to read the story as a rejection of usefulness as such. Boats and coffins must be made from something, and a world of nothing but magnificent useless trees would be a hard place to live. The story's target is narrower and more interesting: the habit of mind that cannot see a tree as anything other than timber not yet cut, and that mistakes the list of its own purposes for an inventory of what the world contains.

options.A: things that are of no use to anyone have no value and are rightly passed by without a second glance.
options.B: every question about what a thing is good for is unreasonable and should be dropped altogether.
options.C: people with conspicuous gifts are likely to be exploited, so wise people avoid drawing attention to themselves.
options.D: craftsmen should learn to find uses even for timber that seems useless at first sight.

questions.question: According to the passage, the usual moral drawn from the story of the tree is that

options.A: a habit of looking at things only for what they can contribute to some purpose beyond themselves.
options.B: a careful study of an object that eventually reveals its hidden and unexpected value.
options.C: a refusal to attend to anything that does not bear fruit or produce food.
options.D: the skill of quickly judging the quality of timber that comes from long practice in a trade.

questions.question: As used in paragraph 3, 'the carpenter's glance' refers to

options.A: It demonstrates that modern institutions are wrong to ask what subjects of study or land are good for.
options.B: It shows that things are valuable in proportion to how little they can be used by people.
options.C: It is mainly practical advice that talented people should hide their gifts in order to survive in a dangerous world.
options.D: Its chief target is a way of seeing that reduces things to their usefulness to someone, not usefulness itself.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the author's main claim about the story of the tree?

options.A: The carpenter, waking from his dream, refuses to let his apprentice cut the tree down and reflects at length that he had misjudged it from the start.
options.B: The tree admits it would gladly have become timber had that been safe, and values its uselessness only as a way of staying alive.
options.C: Travellers continue to rest in the shade of the great tree for many generations after the carpenter's death.
options.D: On waking, the carpenter tells his dream to the apprentice, who doubts whether a tree could ever really speak to anyone.

passage: Before the railways, every town kept its own time. Noon was the moment the sun stood highest over the local meridian, and because the sun appears to move westward, a town some distance to the west of another reached its noon a few minutes later. Nobody minded, because nothing travelled fast enough for the difference to matter; a coach journey of several days absorbed a quarter of an hour's discrepancy without anyone noticing it. The railway changed this, and the standard account of what followed is a story of practical necessity. Timetables drawn up in dozens of local times produced confusion and, on single-track lines, danger, so the companies adopted a single reference time and governments eventually followed.

The account is true as far as it goes, but it treats the change as a technical adjustment, like agreeing on a common gauge for the rails. It was more than that. Local time had been public in a literal sense: anyone could see the sun, and the clock on the church or the town hall was set by an observation that a curious citizen could, in principle, check. Standard time was set somewhere else, by astronomers in a distant observatory, and reached the town along a telegraph wire. The hour on the station clock was no longer a fact about the place where one stood but a decision taken elsewhere and transmitted to it.

This helps to explain a resistance that is usually remembered only as quaint. Some towns kept two clocks running side by side, or fitted a public dial with an extra hand so that the sun's reckoning and the railway's could be read together, and some local worthies denounced the new hour as an imposition. It is easy to read them as people clinging to habit in the face of progress. But they had grasped something that the language of convenience obscures: a shared standard is also a centre of authority, and agreeing to it means accepting that the definition of an everyday reality will henceforth be made by people one will never meet.

None of this is a case against standard time, whose benefits were real and soon taken for granted. Few people today would wish to return to a world in which the hour changed as one rode across a county. The argument is rather that the history of timekeeping is also a history of who is entitled to say what time it is, and that this question did not disappear when it was settled. Each later standard, from time signals broadcast by radio to the clocks that now synchronise themselves silently over networks, has extended the same arrangement, and each has made it a little harder to notice.

options.A: few people owned clocks, so the hour of noon was a matter of rough guesswork in every town alike.
options.B: most towns took their time from the same distant observatory, so that their clocks seldom disagreed by much.
options.C: travel between towns was too slow for a discrepancy of a few minutes to have any practical effect.
options.D: church authorities in each town insisted that the local hour be kept and discouraged comparison with other places.

passage: Suppose a lender uses a scoring system to estimate how likely each applicant is to default, and suppose applicants belong to two groups that differ, for whatever historical reasons, in how often their members in fact default. There are several natural ways to ask whether the system treats the groups fairly. One may ask whether a given score means the same thing in both groups, so that among applicants scored as having a one-in-five chance of default, roughly one in five defaults whichever group they belong to. One may ask instead whether applicants who would in fact have repaid are wrongly refused at the same rate in both groups, or whether those who would in fact have defaulted are wrongly approved at the same rate. Each of these looks like a reasonable requirement, and each has been proposed as the meaning of fairness.

It turns out that they cannot, in general, all be satisfied together. When the groups' underlying default rates differ and the prediction is less than perfect, a score that means the same thing in both groups will produce different rates of error between them, in wrongful refusals, wrongful approvals or both, and equalising both kinds of error will make the same score mean different things in different groups. This is not a defect of any particular system that better engineering might remove; it follows from the arithmetic of prediction under unequal base rates. The finding was greeted in some quarters as a kind of scandal, and two conclusions were quickly drawn from it: that the idea of a fair algorithm is incoherent, or, conversely, that since some criterion must be chosen, the choice is a technical matter best left to the people who build the systems.

Both conclusions seem to me mistaken, and for related reasons. The impossibility does not show that fairness is incoherent; it shows that our everyday notion of fairness bundles together several demands that usually travel together and part company only under specific conditions. Discovering that two values can conflict is not the same as discovering that one of them is empty, any more than the occasional conflict between honesty and kindness shows that one of these is an illusion. Nor does the need to choose make the choice technical. Which criterion should give way depends on what the decision does to the people it touches: who bears the cost of being wrongly refused, how severe that cost is, and whether the different base rates are themselves the residue of earlier unfairness that the decision would perpetuate. Those are questions about harm and responsibility, not about arithmetic.

It is worth adding that the dilemma is not peculiar to algorithms. A loan officer who judges applicants by experience faces exactly the same trade-off whenever the groups differ in base rates; the officer simply does not have to declare which criterion is being sacrificed, and may not know. In this respect the formal analysis has done something valuable. By making the conflict explicit, it has turned a choice that was always being made silently into one that must be made in the open, and has removed the comfortable belief that a sufficiently careful decision maker could satisfy every reasonable demand at once. The danger is that the explicitness is squandered, that the choice is buried again inside the system, this time under a layer of technical vocabulary instead of a layer of personal discretion.

options.A: should favour whichever criterion produces the smallest total number of errors across both groups combined.
options.B: should be left to those who build the scoring system, since they understand the arithmetic of prediction best.
options.C: would rest partly on how heavily each kind of mistaken decision falls on those who must bear it.
options.D: cannot be made on any principled basis, because the competing criteria have been shown to be incompatible.

questions.question: The author would most likely agree that the decision about which fairness criterion should give way

passage: The familiar explanation of teenage recklessness is ignorance: adolescents take risks because they do not understand the dangers, or because they believe, in some half-formed way, that harm happens only to other people. If that were the whole story, the remedy would be straightforward. Teach young people the facts about speeding, drugs and unprotected sex, and their behaviour should improve. Schools and governments have spent heavily on precisely this remedy, and its results have often been modest.

One reason is that the premise is weaker than it looks. When adolescents are asked, in a calm setting, to estimate the dangers of various activities, their answers are often not very different from those of adults, and by the middle teens many reason about risk in hypothetical cases about as well as their parents do. What distinguishes them is less what they know than what happens to that knowledge in particular situations. Decisions taken alone and at leisure look quite mature; decisions taken in the company of friends, under excitement, look very different. In laboratory games that reward bold choices, adolescents have been found to take noticeably more chances when they know their friends are watching, while the presence of an audience makes much less difference to adults.

A plausible account of this pattern appeals to the uneven timing of development. The systems that make rewards, and especially social rewards, feel intense appear to become more responsive around puberty, while the capacities for restraint and planning continue to mature into the early twenties. For several years, then, the accelerator is more sensitive than the brake, and the gap shows most clearly when peers raise the value of a daring act. It should be said that accounts of this kind are easily overstated. Brains do not determine behaviour on their own, adolescents differ widely, and plenty of teenagers who are surrounded by friends behave with conspicuous care.

If the account is broadly right, it has an uncomfortable implication for policy: the most effective interventions may be those that change the situations adolescents find themselves in rather than the beliefs they carry into them. Rules that limit the number of young passengers a new driver may carry, or arrangements that make the safe choice the socially easy one, work with the grain of adolescent decision-making rather than against it. The account also suggests a more generous reading of adolescence itself. A heightened sensitivity to peers is not simply a defect awaiting repair; it is part of what drives young people to leave the family, form their own alliances and try what their elders would not. The same disposition that makes a reckless dare attractive makes new friendships and new ideas attractive too.

options.A: try to supply missing knowledge, when the difficulty lies largely in how knowledge is used in certain situations.
options.B: assume a capacity to apply general facts to one's own conduct that most adolescents do not yet possess.
options.C: have usually given adolescents information about risks that is inaccurate or deliberately exaggerated.
options.D: come from schools and governments, sources whose advice adolescents are inclined to distrust and ignore.

passage: Two complaints about digital information circulate side by side, and at first sight they cannot both be true. The first is that the internet never forgets: an embarrassing photograph or an ill-judged remark, once posted, may resurface years later, copied onto sites its author has never heard of. The second is that digital records are alarmingly fragile: web pages vanish, links lead nowhere, and files saved in formats that no current program can read become, for practical purposes, meaningless strings of bits. One might expect a medium to be either durable or perishable, and it is puzzling to hear the same medium accused of both.

The puzzle dissolves once we stop asking about the medium and start asking about copying. A single digital copy is, if anything, more perishable than a sheet of paper. Paper survives neglect; a letter left in a drawer can usually be read a century later by anyone who knows the language. A file left on an old disk depends on the disk surviving, on a machine that can still read the disk, and on software that can still interpret the file, and each of these dependencies decays on its own schedule. What digital information has, and paper largely lacks, is the capacity to be copied perfectly, instantly and at almost no cost. Its persistence therefore depends far less on the durability of any one copy than on whether enough people, or enough systems, have reasons to keep making copies.

Seen in this light, the two complaints describe the same mechanism working on different material. The embarrassing photograph persists because it is the kind of thing people want to pass on, so it is duplicated faster than any single copy can be deleted. The municipal report, the small society's newsletter and the scholar's personal website persist only as long as someone pays for the server and remembers to renew the domain, because few people have any reason to copy them. Nothing about these documents makes them harder to store than the photograph; a newsletter occupies less space than most images. What they lack is a constituency of copiers. When the society disbands or the scholar retires, the single copy that existed sits on a server whose bills no one is paying, and one day it is simply gone, often without anyone noticing that it has happened. Digital persistence, in short, tracks attention and interest rather than value, and the material most likely to vanish is often the unglamorous record that matters most to a historian a generation later.

This suggests that preservation in a digital age is less a technical problem than an institutional one. Better storage media help, but no medium keeps information alive by itself; what keeps it alive is an organisation that has made copying it someone's duty, and that will go on paying for that duty when the material has ceased to be interesting. Libraries and archives have long performed this role for print, and some are trying to perform it for the web. It is tempting to hope that automated tools, which can gather enormous quantities of web pages without human effort, have made such institutions unnecessary. They have not: what such tools gather must still be stored, checked and kept readable as formats change, and someone must decide what deserves that continuing expense. Archives face a difficulty that print archives faced less acutely: the sheer volume of material means that they must choose, and every choice about what to copy is also, in effect, a choice about what to let disappear. The task cannot be avoided by declaring that everything is saved, because what is left to the accidents of attention is saved very unevenly.

options.A: The belief that the internet never forgets is a myth, since nearly everything posted online eventually disappears without a trace.
options.B: Whether digital material lasts turns on reasons to copy it, which explains both complaints and makes preservation an institutional task.
options.C: Digital records are far less durable than paper and should be printed out whenever they need to be kept for the long term.
options.D: Libraries and archives should copy everything that appears on the web so that no record of the present is ever lost to historians.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the central argument of the passage?

passage: A country that puts a serious price on carbon faces an awkward possibility. If its steelmakers, cement works and chemical firms must pay for their emissions while their competitors abroad do not, production may move to places where emitting is free. The country's own emissions fall, but the world's do not, and some of its industry has been lost for nothing. Economists call this leakage, and fear of it has been among the most effective arguments against acting alone. The obvious answer is a border adjustment: a charge on imports equal to the carbon price that would have been paid had the goods been made at home, perhaps paired with a rebate for exporters. Domestic and foreign producers would then compete on equal terms, and the incentive to relocate would disappear.

The proposal is simpler to state than to carry out. To charge an import for its carbon, one must know how much carbon went into making it, and that depends on the plant, the fuel it burned and the electricity grid it drew from, none of which an importing government can observe directly. Default values can be assigned by product and by country, but these penalise clean producers in dirty countries and reward dirty producers in clean ones. Letting producers prove their actual emissions instead requires inspectors or trusted certifiers inside the exporting country, which raises questions of sovereignty as well as of cost. Trading partners, moreover, are apt to see the charge as protection dressed in green, and some have a further complaint: that countries which grew rich by burning carbon for two centuries are now taxing the goods of countries trying to do the same, and calling it fairness.

There is also reason to think the problem itself has been overstated. For most industries the cost of carbon is a small share of total costs beside labour, transport, access to markets and the quality of local institutions, and firms do not move plants lightly. A steelworks embodies decades of investment in a site, a workforce and a web of local suppliers, and escaping a modest carbon price would seldom justify abandoning all of that. The evidence from carbon prices so far suggests less relocation than the warnings predicted, though the prices in question have mostly been modest and some heavy industries have been shielded from them by free allowances, so the past may be a poor guide to the effect of prices high enough to matter.

If leakage is less of a threat than feared, why does the border adjustment matter? Its most important effect may lie not in the trade it reshapes but in the decisions it prompts elsewhere. An exporting country whose firms face a charge at the border has a reason to prefer that its own government levy an equivalent price at home, so that the revenue stays at home instead of flowing to a foreign treasury. A border adjustment can thus act less as a wall than as a lever, drawing other countries towards carbon pricing of their own. Whether it does so, or instead provokes retaliation, depends heavily on how it is designed and presented. A charge that credits carbon prices already paid abroad, that measures actual emissions where producers can show them, and that directs some of its revenue to helping poorer exporters cut their emissions has a chance of being accepted as what it claims to be. One that does none of these things will be read, not unreasonably, as the protectionism its critics allege.

options.A: is reduced or waived for goods whose makers have already paid a carbon price in their own country.
options.B: lets the importing country keep all of its revenue, so that it can be spent on reducing emissions at home.
options.C: applies only to trading partners whose own carbon prices are already as high as the importing country's price.
options.D: is set high enough to stop most imports from countries that have not yet introduced a price on carbon.
